about.intro: I grew up in Larchmont Falls, where the paper mill whistle doubled as the school bell, and studied statistics at Fernhollow University. In 2020 I became a business analyst at Pinewick Paper & Print, at a desk beside Dennis Hale's rounding-rules binder, and I stayed five years. Two questions took up nearly all of it: were our delivery promises honest, and were our promotion tests telling the truth? I began a PGP at Alder Hall School of Management in 2025, since leading an analytics team needs more than clean SQL.
about.now: Wrapping up a public notebook on the Larchmont river gauges, singing with a small choir on Sunday evenings, and being beaten by the Sunday cryptic more often than not.

eta-accuracy.context: Each Pinewick order shows a promised delivery day at checkout and refreshes it until the van arrives. Three pieces make up the promise: depot pick-and-dispatch time, the truck's journey to the customer's town, and the final drop. As of 2023, the dispatch piece used each depot's four-week average.
eta-accuracy.problem: Our northern-region error breakdown put 61% of squared promise error on dispatch time, worst during the back-to-school rush and on snow days when depots are swamped. In the pilot depots 11.2% of orders arrived after the promised day, which fed a large chunk of 'where is my delivery' calls, most of them landing on Tilly Brandt's desk.
what_i_did: Split promise error by component, day, depot and weather across 640,000 orders, which pointed at dispatch time as the largest and most fixable piece.
Trained a LightGBM model of dispatch time from live signals: the depot's pick queue, recent pick times, lines per order and day of week.
Tested calibration by depot size and day of week, then capped any single update so a model miss could shift a promise by six hours at most.
Planned a staggered rollout over five pilot depots, flipping between old and new model on alternate weeks so weather and the school rush hit both arms alike.
Drafted the rollout with the fulfilment PM, ML engineer and Wendell Odom: five depots, then the northern region, then two southern depots, each step with a weekly error report.

decisions.choice: Alternating weeks, not a customer-level A/B test
decisions.why: Pickers and trucks are shared by every customer in a depot. Giving half the customers new promises would reshuffle the pick order for all of them and spoil the control group.
It carried 61% of the error, and it was the one piece we could fix without touching truck routing, which belonged to another team.

decisions.choice: Cap each promise change at six hours
decisions.why: A promise that lurches annoys customers more than one that is slightly off. Capping the change gave up very little accuracy.

results.note: five pilot depots, six-week alternating rollout

results.metric: Orders delivered after the promised day

eta-accuracy.learned: Building the model was straightforward. Agreeing on what 'better' meant with three teams and one philosophical foreman took far longer, and the alternating-week design is what won them over.
eta-accuracy.next: Apply live queue data to the truck leg, beginning with the long run to the coastal towns where deliveries slip most.
eta-accuracy.my_role: Senior Business Analyst; the analysis, the dispatch-time model and the test design were mine

growly-sip-stops.context: A Brightfold Office Direct standing order ships the same bundle of supplies to an office each month and bills the account automatically. The standing-orders team wanted to know which live orders were about to lapse, and whether any simple step could keep more of them going.
growly-sip-stops.problem: Around 9% of live standing orders lapsed within 60 days. The existing rule only raised a flag after two failed deliveries, typically too late, since the customer had usually decided to leave by then.
what_i_did: Assembled a monthly snapshot of 1.2 million live standing orders with 60-day lapse labels, making sure no feature drew on anything after the snapshot date.
Worked through candidate features with the account team: failed deliveries, delivery day against office opening days, invoice disputes, changes in order size and account age.
Fitted a LightGBM model and scored it on a later month instead of a random split, because back-to-school season shifts buying from one month to the next.
Discovered that 29% of lapses followed a failed delivery on a day the office was closed, and suggested a prompt inviting customers to change their delivery day.
Ran a randomised two-week trial of the prompt on 14,000 accounts with a failed delivery, with wording approved by the account team and legal.

decisions.choice: Score on a later month rather than a random split
decisions.why: A random split scored AUC 0.81, but it lets seasonal patterns leak between training and test data. The later month scored 0.74, which is what the team should plan on.

decisions.choice: Try a single inexpensive remedy, not a retention campaign
decisions.why: The model surfaced one big, well-defined group. A delivery-day prompt needs no discount or new screens, so an intern could test it in ten weeks.

results.note: held-out month, vs 0.63 for the two-failed-deliveries rule

results.metric: Lapses caught in top 10% of scores

growly-sip-stops.learned: The score mattered less than the explanation of why accounts lapsed. The closed-office clash sat in the data for years, waiting for someone to put delivery days next to opening days.
growly-sip-stops.next: Follow moved orders through a whole billing cycle to see whether they stay active past month one, then try the score as a trigger for account-team calls.
growly-sip-stops.my_role: Data Science Intern, responsible for the model and the trial analysis

larkspur-air.context: Each spring the Larchmont river swells with snowmelt, and each town meeting argument cites a different gauge. The county posts hourly levels for six gauges in the valley, though the files contain holes, changed units and frozen sensors.
larkspur-air.problem: Nobody had published a tidy comparison of the six gauges across several springs, or checked how closely a gauge matches the water level at the spots people worry about.
what_i_did: Pulled six years of hourly readings (2019–2025) for the six gauges and coded checks for gaps, repeats and abrupt jumps, which removed about 8% of hours.
Compared gauges by month and time of day, and set aside rain effects using public rainfall and snow-depth records.
Walked a three-kilometre bank with a marked depth stick for three weeks in April 2025, recording 38 visits.
Checked the stick against the Millrace Bridge gauge for a week before starting, and carried that error band into every reading reported.
Released the notebook on DataArena and GitHub with a plain summary, then talked the river-watch volunteers through it.

decisions.choice: Discard bad hours rather than patching them
decisions.why: Interpolating across the melt would have flattened the very peaks the notebook studies. I reported each gauge's share of dropped hours instead.

decisions.choice: Show the stick data with its error band
decisions.why: A marked stick is no reference instrument. Printing its calibration error alongside the readings kept the comparison fair.

results.note: April average across gauges, midnight–4 am vs 1–4 pm
DataArena and GitHub, first three months

larkspur-air.learned: Deciding which readings to distrust was the bulk of the job. The gauge that looked worst on most days turned out to have a sensor frozen on one value for 9 days in 2023.
larkspur-air.next: Bring in bank readings from two volunteers on other stretches, and check whether the peak moved after the 2024 upstream weir repairs.

eta-accuracy.q: What causes delivery-promise error, and how much can be taken out?
eta-accuracy.sql:
-- share of squared promise error by component, northern region
SELECT component,
       SUM(err_hrs * err_hrs)
         / SUM(SUM(err_hrs * err_hrs)) OVER () AS share_sq_err
FROM   promise_error_components
WHERE  region = 'NORTH'
GROUP  BY component
ORDER  BY share_sq_err DESC;

growly-sip-stops.q: Which standing orders lapse within 60 days, and can one inexpensive remedy help?
growly-sip-stops.sql:
-- failed deliveries where the delivery day is an office closed day
SELECT s.order_id,
       s.delivery_dow,
       o.closed_dow,
       s.delivery_dow = o.closed_dow AS delivered_when_closed
FROM   standing_snapshot s
JOIN   office_calendar o USING (account_id)
WHERE  s.snapshot_month = '2026-04-01'
  AND  s.failed_delivery_30d;

larkspur-air.q: Which of the six valley river gauges is safe to quote, and what escapes them?
larkspur-air.sql:
-- melt-night vs afternoon rise, valid hours only
SELECT gauge,
       AVG(rise_cm) FILTER (WHERE hour BETWEEN 0 AND 4) /
       AVG(rise_cm) FILTER (WHERE hour BETWEEN 13 AND 16) AS night_ratio,
       AVG((NOT valid)::int) AS share_dropped
FROM   county_hourly
WHERE  month = 4
GROUP  BY gauge;

experiment-review.q: What share of our test results deserved trust?
experiment-review.sql:
-- split-ratio check before anyone reads the result
SELECT test_id,
       SUM((arm = 'control')::int)   AS n_control,
       SUM((arm = 'treatment')::int) AS n_treatment,
       chi2_srm(n_control, n_treatment, 0.5) AS p_srm
FROM   assignments
GROUP  BY test_id
HAVING chi2_srm(n_control, n_treatment, 0.5) < 0.001;

datathon.q: Can term-start weeks and monsoon days be modelled rather than dismissed as noise?
datathon.sql:
-- next-day demand features per SKU and wholesale depot
SELECT depot_id, sku_id, dt,
       units,
       is_term_start,
       rain_mm > 5 AS rain_day,
       AVG(units) OVER w7 AS units_7d
FROM   daily_sku_demand
WINDOW w7 AS (PARTITION BY depot_id, sku_id
              ORDER BY dt ROWS 7 PRECEDING);

active-subscriber.q: Why were four different active-account counts reaching the board?
active-subscriber.sql:
-- single definition, checked against each old figure
SELECT month_end,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE plan_status = 'paid'
                          AND NOT paused
                          AND next_box <= month_end + 35) AS active_accounts
FROM   accounts_monthly
GROUP  BY month_end;

home-credit-dataarena.q: Which features hold steady week on week, rather than on one split alone?
home-credit-dataarena.sql:
# keep features whose weekly Gini does not drift
stable = (weekly_gini
          .groupby('feature')['gini']
          .agg(['mean', 'std'])
          .query('std < 0.02'))
kept = stable.index.tolist()   # 190 of 410

small-samples.q: Can a broken test be explained every fortnight to readers who are not analysts?
small-samples.sql:
-- newsletter, since 2024
SELECT COUNT(*)            AS posts,        -- 24
       MAX(subscribers)    AS subscribers,  -- 940
       AVG(open_rate)      AS open_rate     -- 0.44
FROM   small_samples.posts;

glossary.def: Any account on a paid plan, not paused, with a box due inside 35 days of the month end. Counted once, on the month's final day.
Average absolute gap, in hours, between the dispatch time implied by the checkout promise and real dispatch, worked out per order and then averaged.
Delivered after the day promised at checkout. Revised promises do not restart the clock.
The actual customer split between arms strays from the planned split further than chance explains (chi-square p < 0.001). A failed check means nobody reads the result.
A measure that cannot slip if a launch is to proceed, whatever the headline metric does. For sales pods: returns, late deliveries and margin per order.
The least real change a test is built to spot, at 80% power and a 5% false-alarm rate. Fixed beforehand from what would justify shipping.
Old and new versions swap by week inside one depot, so pickers and trucks shared between them cannot contaminate the control.
How well a model ranks cases in a calendar month later than its training data. It reads lower than a random split and nearer to real use.
Total absolute forecast error over total actual demand, so high-volume SKUs weigh more than slow sellers.
An hourly river reading discarded because the sensor froze on one value, showed zero, or leapt past physical limits. Counted per gauge and never patched.
